Bloomberg previously shared initial details about OpenAI's first smart device, and now a new report has revealed more information about its design and pricing. Here's the latest.

OpenAI's speaker may be priced above US$300

A few weeks ago, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI's first device would be a portable speaker with a built-in battery, equipped with a camera and other sensors, and featuring "moving mechanical parts that make it feel alive, rather than just an object that responds to commands".

The report said OpenAI is developing "about five different products," but plans to lead with this speaker, hoping to unveil it within the year and officially launch it in 2027.

Bloomberg added that the timeline could change depending on the outcome of a lawsuit from Apple, which alleges that OpenAI used trade secrets stolen by former Apple employees to develop its upcoming hardware products.

Bloomberg has now further disclosed more details about OpenAI's first device, reporting that the company had discussed pricing it between US$300 and US$400 per unit. The product is expected to have a "premium look," using "high-quality materials such as premium metals," and to be usable around the clock.

The report states:

Bloomberg further noted that the speaker "is designed to be used in different postures," including being held in the user's hand or placed on furniture at home. Its moving parts are intended to make the device feel more alive, while more advanced AI models will support natural, human-like voice interactions similar to ChatGPT's recently improved voice mode.

Today's report coincides with the day OpenAI filed a motion to dismiss Apple's lawsuit. OpenAI's argument is that Apple has failed to identify specific trade secrets and has no basis for allegations of wrongdoing against OpenAI, claiming the complaint takes "general conduct" out of context and was filed "without adequate investigation".

As Bloomberg noted in today's report, the design described "is not something Apple ever came close to releasing," but the use of premium metals could be related to one of the manufacturing-related allegations in Apple's lawsuit. Bloomberg also noted that it remains unclear whether the allegation targets this device, another product, or a concept that has already been shelved.
